title: What the deniers of indifference mean: equipoise, in which no Christian theologian ever placed freedom
source_text: XXVI. Qui vero contra pugnant ad libertatem arbitrii non requiri aliquam agentis indifferentiam, indifferentiae nomine significare videntur voluntatis ἰσοῤῥοπίαν, quum in hanc partem non magis quam in aliam propendet, & huc non magis quam illuc flexilis est, qua in re nullus eorum qui in Scholis Christianis Theologi nomen ferunt, libertatem unquam constituit.
pass_a_gloss: But those who on the contrary contend that some indifference of the agent is not required to liberty of choice, seem by the name of indifference to signify the equipoise (ἰσοῤῥοπία) of the will, when it inclines to this part no more than to another, and is flexible hither no more than thither, in which no one of those who bear the name of Theologian in the Christian Schools, ever placed liberty.
pass_b_english: Those who argue the other way, that freedom of choice does not require any indifference in the agent, seem to mean by indifference the will's equal balance (ἰσοῤῥοπία), when it leans no more to one side than to the other and can be swayed no more this way than that.
Yet no one who bears the name of theologian in the Christian Schools has ever made freedom consist in that.

choices.why: Kept as the Schools' technical term; Le Blanc fixes its sense as a real power to act otherwise, not a state of balance between options.
